- much like how, in the realm of closures, it is done with the

In other words:

`: <'_>`and HKTs are to GATs what closures are to traits.

(it’s the `Fn(Lifetime) -> Type` of the type realm).

Finally, another observation which I find interesting, is that:

```
type A = ForLt!(<'r> = &'r str);
// vs.
type B        <'r> = &'r str;
```
is an annoying limitation of Rust, which happens to feature a similar
distinction that certain past languages have had between values, and
functions, wherein they were treated separately (rather than as first-class
citizens, *i.e.*, like the other values).

In Rust, `type B<'r> = &'r str;` suffers from this same kind of limitation,
only in the type realm this time: `type B<'r> =` is a special construct,
which yields a *“type” constructor*. That is, it yields some syntax, `B`, to
which we can feed a lifetime `'lt`, by writing `B<'lt>`, so as to end up
with a *type*.

**But  B, in and of itself,  is not a type**, even if we often call it a
“generic type” by abuse of terminology.

Which is why it cannot be fed, *alone*, to some type-generic API that would
want to be the one feeding the lifetime parameter: it does not play well
with “generic generics”!

In this example, the only true “generic *type*”, that is, the *type* which
is, itself, lifetime-generic, is `A`.

This is where [ ForLt!](https://docs.rs/macro.ForLt.html) and HKTs, thus, shine.

- For Haskell enthusiasts, this - `: For`-bounded- `… -> *`kind.

 Then, an Arrow-Kinded type which has, inside the- `…`, yet another Arrow-Kinded type, is what is called a Higher-Kinded Type:
 \- [↩](https://docs.rs#fnref1)

The main trait of the crate. The one expressing `: <'_>`-genericity.

It is expected to be used as a bound on a `<T>` generic parameter,

conceptually / sort to speak, is to be read as [ForLt](https://docs.rs/trait.ForLifetime.html)>`<T : <'_>>`.

generic too!**

-

- “Arrow-Kinded Type”: `… -> *`, such as`ForLt!(<'a> = &'a str) : ForLt`.
- Higher-Kinded Type: `(… -> *) -> *`, such as`struct Example<T : ForLt>`.

It cannot be manually implemented: the only types implementing this trait
are the ones produced by the [ ForLt!](https://docs.rs/macro.ForLt.html) macro.

# ForLifetime in higher_kinded_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/higher-kinded-types/0.2.1/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/higher_kinded_types/trait.ForLifetime.html

    type
```
[Of](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Of)<'lt>;
}## Expand description

The main trait of the crate. The one expressing `: <'_>`-genericity.

It is expected to be used as a bound on a `<T>` generic parameter,
thereby resulting in a `<T : ` generic API, which,
conceptually / sort to speak, is to be read as [ForLt](https://docs.rs/trait.ForLifetime.html)>`<T : <'_>>`.

That is, **a  generic API whose generic parameter is, in and of itself,
generic too!**

-
Such a “generic-generic API” is dubbed *higher-kinded*, which makes a type such as`struct Example<T: <'_>>`then be dubbed*higher-kinded type*, or**HKT**, for short.From there, the whole concept of expressing genericity over `: <'_>`-generic types can also be associated with the idea and concept of higher-kinded types, much like the name of this crate indicates.So, using this HKT terminology for something other than a type taking a `: For`-bounded[1](https://docs.rs#fn1)

- “Arrow-Kinded Type”: `… -> *`, such as`ForLt!(<'a> = &'a str) : ForLt`.
- Higher-Kinded Type: `(… -> *) -> *`, such as`struct Example<T : ForLt>`.

It cannot be manually implemented: the only types implementing this trait
are the ones produced by the [ ForLt!](https://docs.rs/macro.ForLt.html) macro.

In a way, the similarity between these two paradigms is akin to that of

canonical object interface, say:

trait Closure<Args> {

and then use `Closure<Args, Ret = …>` where we currently use
`Fn(Args…) -> Output`: that is, the *canonical* `Fn…` traits can easily be
polyfilled with any arbitrary trait of our choice featuring the same
functional API (same method signature).

or, *vice versa*, never define custom traits or interfaces, and always
use closures:

-
The astute reader may notice that we lose the *nominal typing*aspect of our current traits, which is what lets us, for instance, distinguish between`Display`and`Debug`, even if both traits,*structurally*, are equivalent / have exactly the same function signature.- In general, Rust traits go way beyond the sheer API of their
methods. They can be used as (sometimes `unsafe`) marker traits, or other API promises,*etc.*

So, closures are just one specific interface/trait shape, which we could use pervasively everywhere, if we did not mind the loss of “nominal typing” (the trait name).

But they’re actually more: closures would not be near as useful as they are
if we did not have **closure expressions**!

In fact, closure expressions are so handy that nowadays we have a bunch of
`impl Trait` constructors that take the raw/bare API/signature as a closure,
and then wrap it within the “name” of the trait:

- `Iterator`- `FnMut() -> Option<Item>`using- `iter::from_fn()`
- `Future`- `FnMut(&mut`using- [Context](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/task/wake/struct.Context.html)<'_>) ->- [Poll](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/task/poll/enum.Poll.html)<Output>- `future::poll_fn()`
- `Stream`- `FnMut(Acc) -> impl Future<Output = (Item, Acc)>`using- `stream::unfold()`

And that same difference applies to arbitrary GATs *vs.* [ ForLt](https://docs.rs/trait.ForLifetime.html): the
ability to produce

*ad-hoc*/ on-demand

`impl `[ForLt](https://docs.rs/trait.ForLifetime.html) types /

`ForLt`[macro, is what makes](https://docs.rs/macro.ForLt.html)

`ForLt`*vs.*the overly cumbersome aspect of manually using custom GATs.

Finally, another observation which I find interesting, is that:

```
type A = ForLt!(<'r> = &'r str);
// vs.
type B        <'r> = &'r str;
```
is an annoying limitation of Rust, which happens to feature a similar
distinction that certain past languages have had between values, and
functions, wherein they were treated separately (rather than as first-class
citizens, *i.e.*, like the other values).

In Rust, `type B<'r> = &'r str;` suffers from this same kind of limitation,
only in the type realm this time: `type B<'r> =` is a special construct,
which yields a *“type” constructor*. That is, it yields some syntax, `B`, to
which we can feed a lifetime `'lt`, by writing `B<'lt>`, so as to end up
with a *type*.

**But  B, in and of itself,  is not a type**, even if we often call it a
“generic type” by abuse of terminology.

Which is why it cannot be fed, *alone*, to some type-generic API that would
want to be the one feeding the lifetime parameter: it does not play well
with “generic generics”!

In this example, the only true “generic *type*”, that is, the *type* which
is, itself, lifetime-generic, is `A`.

This is where [ ForLt!](https://docs.rs/macro.ForLt.html) and HKTs, thus, shine.

[103](https://docs.rs#103)
[104](https://docs.rs#104)mod with_lifetime {
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    pub
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    trait WithLifetime<'lt>
[107](https://docs.rs#107)    :
[108](https://docs.rs#108)        Send + Sync + Unpin
[109](https://docs.rs#109)    {
[110](https://docs.rs#110)        type T;
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    }
[112](https://docs.rs#112)
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    impl<'lt, T : ?Sized + WithLifetime<'lt>>
[114](https://docs.rs#114)        WithLifetime<'lt>
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    for
[116](https://docs.rs#116)        crate::ඞ::ForLt<T>
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    {
[118](https://docs.rs#118)        type T = T::T;
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    }
[120](https://docs.rs#120)}
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)/// The main trait of the crate. The one expressing `: <'_>`-genericity.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)///
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// It is expected to be used as a bound on a `<T>` generic parameter,
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// thereby resulting in a <code><T : [ForLt]></code> generic API, which,
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// conceptually / sort to speak, is to be read as `<T : <'_>>`.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)///
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// That is, **a _generic API_ whose generic parameter is, in and of itself,
[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// _generic too_!**
[130](https://docs.rs#130)///
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///   - Such a "generic-generic API" is dubbed _higher-kinded_, which makes a
[132](https://docs.rs#132)///     type such as `struct Example<T: <'_>>` then be dubbed _higher-kinded
[133](https://docs.rs#133)///     type_, or **HKT**, for short.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)///
[135](https://docs.rs#135)///     From there, the whole concept of expressing genericity over
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///     `: <'_>`-generic types can also be associated with the idea and concept
[137](https://docs.rs#137)///     of higher-kinded types, much like the name of this crate indicates.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)///
[139](https://docs.rs#139)///     So, using this HKT terminology for something other than a type taking
[140](https://docs.rs#140)///     a [`: For`-bounded] generic type is, if we are to be pedantic[^haskell]
[141](https://docs.rs#141)///     about the topic, an abuse of terminology (one which I'll probably make
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///     throughout this documentation).
[143](https://docs.rs#143)///
[144](https://docs.rs#144)///
[145](https://docs.rs#145)/// [^haskell]: For Haskell enthusiasts, this [`: For`-bounded]-ness could be
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// called "Arrow-Kinded", as in, it matches the `… -> *` kind. \
[147](https://docs.rs#147)/// \
[148](https://docs.rs#148)/// Then, an Arrow-Kinded type which has, inside the `…`, yet another
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// Arrow-Kinded type, is what is called a Higher-Kinded Type: \
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// \
[151](https://docs.rs#151)///   - "Arrow-Kinded Type": `… -> *`, such as `ForLt!(<'a> = &'a str) : ForLt`.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)///   - Higher-Kinded Type: `(… -> *) -> *`, such as `struct Example<T : ForLt>`.
[153](https://docs.rs#153)///
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// [`: For`-bounded]: extra_arities/index.html
[155](https://docs.rs#155)///
[156](https://docs.rs#156)/// [ForLt]: trait@ForLt
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// [`ForLt`]: trait@ForLt
[158](https://docs.rs#158)///
[159](https://docs.rs#159)/// It cannot be manually implemented: the only types implementing this trait
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// are the ones produced by the [`ForLt!`] macro.
[161](https://docs.rs#161)///
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// ## HKT Usage
[163](https://docs.rs#163)///
[164](https://docs.rs#164)///  1. Make your API take a generic <code>\<T : [ForLifetime]\></code>
[165](https://docs.rs#165)///     parameter (conceptually, a <code>\<T : [Ofᐸᑊ_ᐳ]\></code> parameter).
[166](https://docs.rs#166)///
[167](https://docs.rs#167)///     Congratulations, you now have a _higher-kinded_ API: your API is
[168](https://docs.rs#168)///     not only generic, but it is also taking a parameter which is, in turn,
[169](https://docs.rs#169)///     generic.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)///
[171](https://docs.rs#171)///  1. #### Callers
[172](https://docs.rs#172)///
[173](https://docs.rs#173)///     Call sites use the [`ForLt!`] macro to produce a type which they
[174](https://docs.rs#174)///     can _and must_ turbofish to such APIs. For instance:
[175](https://docs.rs#175)///
[176](https://docs.rs#176)///       - <code>[ForLt!]\(&str\)</code> for the pervasive reference case
[177](https://docs.rs#177)///         (which could also use the <code>[ForRef]\<str\></code> type alias
[178](https://docs.rs#178)///         to avoid the macro),
[179](https://docs.rs#179)///
[180](https://docs.rs#180)///         or <code>[ForLt!]\(Cow\<\'_, str\>\)</code> for more complex
[181](https://docs.rs#181)///         lifetime-infected types;
[182](https://docs.rs#182)///
[183](https://docs.rs#183)///       - <code>[ForLt!]\(u8\)</code> or other owned types work too: it is not
[184](https://docs.rs#184)///         mandatory, at the call-site, to be lifetime-infected, it is just
[185](https://docs.rs#185)///         _possible_ (maximally flexible API). See [`ForFixed`].
[186](https://docs.rs#186)///
[187](https://docs.rs#187)///  1. #### Callee/API author
[188](https://docs.rs#188)///
[189](https://docs.rs#189)///     Make use of this nested genericity in your API!
[190](https://docs.rs#190)///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)///     Feed, somewhere, a lifetime parameter to this `T`:
[192](https://docs.rs#192)///
[193](https://docs.rs#193)///     ```rust
[194](https://docs.rs#194)///     # #[cfg(any())] macro_rules! ignore {
[195](https://docs.rs#195)///     T::Of<'some_lifetime_param>
[196](https://docs.rs#196)///     # }
[197](https://docs.rs#197)///     ```
[198](https://docs.rs#198)///
[199](https://docs.rs#199)///     There are two situations where this is handy:
[200](https://docs.rs#200)///
[201](https://docs.rs#201)///       - wanting to feed two different lifetimes to `T`:
[202](https://docs.rs#202)///
[203](https://docs.rs#203)///          ```rust
[204](https://docs.rs#204)///          use ::higher_kinded_types::ForLifetime;
[205](https://docs.rs#205)///
[206](https://docs.rs#206)///          struct Example<'a, 'b, T : ForLifetime> {
[207](https://docs.rs#207)///              a: T::Of<'a>,
[208](https://docs.rs#208)///              b: T::Of<'b>,
[209](https://docs.rs#209)///          }
[210](https://docs.rs#210)///          ```
[211](https://docs.rs#211)///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)///       - wanting to "feed a lifetime later" / to feed a
[213](https://docs.rs#213)///         `for<>`-quantified lifetime to your <code>impl [ForLt]</code> type:
[214](https://docs.rs#214)///
[215](https://docs.rs#215)///          ```rust
[216](https://docs.rs#216)///          # #[cfg(any())] macro_rules! ignore {
[217](https://docs.rs#217)///          use ::higher_kinded_types::ForLifetime as Ofᐸᑊ_ᐳ; // hopefully illustrative renaming.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)///          fn slice_sort_by_key<Item, Key : Ofᐸᑊ_ᐳ> (
[220](https://docs.rs#220)///              items: &'_ mut [Item],
[221](https://docs.rs#221)///              mut get_key: impl FnMut(&'_ Item) -> Key::Of<'_>,
[222](https://docs.rs#222)///          )
[223](https://docs.rs#223)///          # }
[224](https://docs.rs#224)///          ```
[225](https://docs.rs#225)///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)///          Full example:
[227](https://docs.rs#227)///
[228](https://docs.rs#228)///          <details class="custom"><summary><span class="summary-box"><span>Click to show</span></span></summary>
[229](https://docs.rs#229)///
[230](https://docs.rs#230)///          ```rust
[231](https://docs.rs#231)///          use ::higher_kinded_types::ForLt;
[232](https://docs.rs#232)///
[233](https://docs.rs#233)///          fn slice_sort_by_key<Item, Key : ForLt> (
[234](https://docs.rs#234)///              items: &'_ mut [Item],
[235](https://docs.rs#235)///              mut get_key: impl for<'it> FnMut(&'it Item) -> Key::Of<'it>,
[236](https://docs.rs#236)///          )
[237](https://docs.rs#237)///          where
[238](https://docs.rs#238)///              for<'it> Key::Of<'it> : Ord,
[239](https://docs.rs#239)///          {
[240](https://docs.rs#240)///              items.sort_by(|a: &'_ Item, b: &'_ Item| <Key::Of<'_>>::cmp(
[241](https://docs.rs#241)///                  &get_key(a),
[242](https://docs.rs#242)///                  &get_key(b),
[243](https://docs.rs#243)///              ))
[244](https://docs.rs#244)///          }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)///
[246](https://docs.rs#246)///          // Demo:
[247](https://docs.rs#247)///          let clients: &mut [Client] = // …;
[248](https://docs.rs#248)///          # &mut []; struct Client { key: String, version: u8 }
[249](https://docs.rs#249)///
[250](https://docs.rs#250)///          slice_sort_by_key::<_, ForLt!(&str)>(clients, |c| &c.key); // ✅
[251](https://docs.rs#251)///
[252](https://docs.rs#252)///          // Important: owned case works too!
[253](https://docs.rs#253)///          slice_sort_by_key::<_, ForLt!(u8)>(clients, |c| c.version); // ✅
[254](https://docs.rs#254)///
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///          # #[cfg(any())] {
[256](https://docs.rs#256)///          // But the classic `sort_by_key` stdlib API fails, since it does not use HKTs:
[257](https://docs.rs#257)///          clients.sort_by_key(|c| &c.key); // ❌ Error: cannot infer an appropriate lifetime for autoref due to conflicting requirements
[258](https://docs.rs#258)///          # }
[259](https://docs.rs#259)///          ```
[260](https://docs.rs#260)///
[261](https://docs.rs#261)///          </details>
[262](https://docs.rs#262)///
[263](https://docs.rs#263)/// ### Wait a moment; this is just a GAT! Why are you talking of HKTs?
[264](https://docs.rs#264)///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)/// Indeed, the definition of the <code>[ForLt]</code> trait is basically that
[266](https://docs.rs#266)/// of a trait featuring the simplest possible GAT:
[267](https://docs.rs#267)///
[268](https://docs.rs#268)/// ```rust
[269](https://docs.rs#269)/// trait Trait { // basic trait
[270](https://docs.rs#270)///     type Assoc<'lt>; // Associated Type which is itself Generic = GAT.
[271](https://docs.rs#271)/// }
[272](https://docs.rs#272)///
[273](https://docs.rs#273)/// struct Struct<'a, 'b, T : Trait> {
[274](https://docs.rs#274)///     a: T::Assoc<'a>,
[275](https://docs.rs#275)///     b: T::Assoc<'b>,
[276](https://docs.rs#276)/// }
[277](https://docs.rs#277)/// ```
[278](https://docs.rs#278)///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)/// Yes, the `: <'_>` signature pattern of HKTs, and GATs, from this point of
[280](https://docs.rs#280)/// view, are quite interchangeable:
[281](https://docs.rs#281)///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)///   - this whole crate is a demonstration of featuring `: <'_>` HKT idioms
[283](https://docs.rs#283)///     through a [`ForLt`] GAT trait (+ some extra `for<>`-quantifications);
[284](https://docs.rs#284)///
[285](https://docs.rs#285)///   - in a world with HKTs and `: <'_>` as a first-class construct, GATs could
[286](https://docs.rs#286)///     then just be HKT Associated Types (HATs instead of GATs 🤠).
[287](https://docs.rs#287)///
[288](https://docs.rs#288)///     ```rust ,ignore
[289](https://docs.rs#289)///     //! pseudo-code!
[290](https://docs.rs#290)///     trait LendingIterator {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)///         type Item: <'_>;
[292](https://docs.rs#292)///
[293](https://docs.rs#293)///         fn next(&mut self) -> Self::Item<'_>;
[294](https://docs.rs#294)///     }
[295](https://docs.rs#295)///     ```
[296](https://docs.rs#296)///
[297](https://docs.rs#297)///       - Real code:
[298](https://docs.rs#298)///
[299](https://docs.rs#299)///         <details class="custom"><summary><span class="summary-box"><span>Click to show</span></span></summary>
[300](https://docs.rs#300)///
[301](https://docs.rs#301)///         ```rust
[302](https://docs.rs#302)///         use ::higher_kinded_types::ForLt;
[303](https://docs.rs#303)///
[304](https://docs.rs#304)///         trait LendingIterator {
[305](https://docs.rs#305)///             /// Look ma, "no" GATs!
[306](https://docs.rs#306)///             type Item: ForLt;
[307](https://docs.rs#307)///
[308](https://docs.rs#308)///             fn next(&mut self) -> <Self::Item as ForLt>::Of<'_>;
[309](https://docs.rs#309)///         }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)///         ```
[311](https://docs.rs#311)///
[312](https://docs.rs#312)///     </details>
[313](https://docs.rs#313)///
[314](https://docs.rs#314)/// In a way, the similarity between these two paradigms is akin to that of
[315](https://docs.rs#315)/// closure _vs._ object in more classic programming: you can always pick some
[316](https://docs.rs#316)/// canonical object interface, say:
[317](https://docs.rs#317)///
[318](https://docs.rs#318)/// ```rust
[319](https://docs.rs#319)/// trait Closure<Args> {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)///     type Ret;
[321](https://docs.rs#321)///
[322](https://docs.rs#322)///     fn call(&self, _: Args) -> Self::Ret;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)/// }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)/// ```
[325](https://docs.rs#325)///
[326](https://docs.rs#326)/// and then use `Closure<Args, Ret = …>` where we currently use
[327](https://docs.rs#327)/// `Fn(Args…) -> Output`: that is, the _canonical_ `Fn…` traits can easily be
[328](https://docs.rs#328)/// polyfilled with any arbitrary trait of our choice featuring the same
[329](https://docs.rs#329)/// functional API (same method signature).
[330](https://docs.rs#330)///
[331](https://docs.rs#331)/// or, _vice versa_, never define custom traits or interfaces, and always
[332](https://docs.rs#332)/// use closures:
[333](https://docs.rs#333)///
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// ```rust ,ignore
[335](https://docs.rs#335)/// trait Display = Fn(&mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result;
[336](https://docs.rs#336)/// // etc.
[337](https://docs.rs#337)/// ```
[338](https://docs.rs#338)///
[339](https://docs.rs#339)///   - The astute reader may notice that we lose the _nominal typing_ aspect
[340](https://docs.rs#340)///     of our current traits, which is what lets us, for instance, distinguish
[341](https://docs.rs#341)///     between `Display` and `Debug`, even if both traits, _structurally_, are
[342](https://docs.rs#342)///     equivalent / have exactly the same function signature.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)///
[344](https://docs.rs#344)///       - In general, Rust traits go way beyond the sheer API of their
[345](https://docs.rs#345)///         methods. They can be used as (sometimes `unsafe`) marker traits, or
[346](https://docs.rs#346)///         other API promises, _etc._
[347](https://docs.rs#347)///
[348](https://docs.rs#348)/// So, closures are just one specific interface/trait shape, which we could use
[349](https://docs.rs#349)/// pervasively everywhere, if we did not mind the loss of "nominal typing" (the
[350](https://docs.rs#350)/// trait name).
[351](https://docs.rs#351)///
[352](https://docs.rs#352)/// But they're actually more: closures would not be near as useful as they are
[353](https://docs.rs#353)/// if we did not have **closure expressions**!
[354](https://docs.rs#354)///
[355](https://docs.rs#355)/// In fact, closure expressions are so handy that nowadays we have a bunch of
[356](https://docs.rs#356)/// `impl Trait` constructors that take the raw/bare API/signature as a closure,
[357](https://docs.rs#357)/// and then wrap it within the "name" of the trait:
[358](https://docs.rs#358)///
[359](https://docs.rs#359)///   - **[`Iterator`]**: from
[360](https://docs.rs#360)///     `FnMut() -> Option<Item>`
[361](https://docs.rs#361)///     using [`iter::from_fn()`][::core::iter::from_fn]
[362](https://docs.rs#362)///   - **[`Future`]**: from
[363](https://docs.rs#363)///     <code>FnMut\(\&mut [Context]\<\'_\>\) -\> [Poll]\<Output\></code>
[364](https://docs.rs#364)///     using [`future::poll_fn()`][::core::future::poll_fn];
[365](https://docs.rs#365)///   - **[`Stream`]**: from
[366](https://docs.rs#366)///     `FnMut(Acc) -> impl Future<Output = (Item, Acc)>`
[367](https://docs.rs#367)///     using [`stream::unfold()`]
[368](https://docs.rs#368)///
[369](https://docs.rs#369)/// [`Future`]: ::core::future::Future
[370](https://docs.rs#370)/// [Context]: ::core::task::Context
[371](https://docs.rs#371)/// [Poll]: ::core::task::Poll
[372](https://docs.rs#372)/// [`Stream`]: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3.28/futures/stream/trait.Stream.html
[373](https://docs.rs#373)/// [`stream::unfold()`]: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3.28/futures/stream/fn.unfold.html
[374](https://docs.rs#374)///
[375](https://docs.rs#375)/// And that same difference applies to arbitrary GATs _vs._ [`ForLt`]: the
[376](https://docs.rs#376)/// ability to produce _ad-hoc_ / on-demand <code>impl [ForLt]</code> types /
[377](https://docs.rs#377)/// [`ForLt`] type "expressions", thanks to the [`ForLt!`] macro, is what makes
[378](https://docs.rs#378)/// [`ForLt`] convenient and flexible, _vs._ the overly cumbersome aspect of
[379](https://docs.rs#379)/// manually using custom GATs.
[380](https://docs.rs#380)///
[381](https://docs.rs#381)/// Indeed, compare:
[382](https://docs.rs#382)///
[383](https://docs.rs#383)/// ```rust
[384](https://docs.rs#384)/// trait ForLt {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)///     type Assoc<'lt>;
[386](https://docs.rs#386)/// }
[387](https://docs.rs#387)///
[388](https://docs.rs#388)/// enum StrRef {}
[389](https://docs.rs#389)///
[390](https://docs.rs#390)/// impl ForLt for StrRef {
[391](https://docs.rs#391)///     type Assoc<'lt> = &'lt str;
[392](https://docs.rs#392)/// }
[393](https://docs.rs#393)/// ```
[394](https://docs.rs#394)///
[395](https://docs.rs#395)/// to:
[396](https://docs.rs#396)///
[397](https://docs.rs#397)/// ```rust
[398](https://docs.rs#398)/// # use ::higher_kinded_types::ForLt;
[399](https://docs.rs#399)/// type StrRef = ForLt!(<'lt> = &'lt str);
[400](https://docs.rs#400)/// ```
[401](https://docs.rs#401)///
[402](https://docs.rs#402)/// ### Conclusion
[403](https://docs.rs#403)///
[404](https://docs.rs#404)/// So, to summarize, this <code>[ForLt] = ": \<\'_\>"</code> HKT pattern is just:
[405](https://docs.rs#405)///
[406](https://docs.rs#406)///   - some GAT API having been _canonical_-ized,
[407](https://docs.rs#407)///
[408](https://docs.rs#408)///       - much like how, in the realm of closures, the `Fn(Args…) -> R` was
[409](https://docs.rs#409)///         picked (_vs._ any other signature-equivalent
[410](https://docs.rs#410)///         `Closure<Args, Ret = R>` trait);
[411](https://docs.rs#411)///
[412](https://docs.rs#412)///   - which can be "inhabited" _on demand_ / in an _ad-hoc_ fashion thanks to
[413](https://docs.rs#413)///     the <code>[ForLt!]\(\<\'input\> = Output…\)</code> macro,
[414](https://docs.rs#414)///
[415](https://docs.rs#415)///       - much like how, in the realm of closures, it is done with the
[416](https://docs.rs#416)///         `|input…| output…` closure expressions.
[417](https://docs.rs#417)///
[418](https://docs.rs#418)/// In other words:
[419](https://docs.rs#419)///
[420](https://docs.rs#420)/// > `: <'_>` and HKTs are to GATs what closures are to traits.
[421](https://docs.rs#421)///
[422](https://docs.rs#422)/// (it's the `Fn(Lifetime) -> Type` of the type realm).
[423](https://docs.rs#423)///
[424](https://docs.rs#424)/// ___
[425](https://docs.rs#425)///
[426](https://docs.rs#426)/// Finally, another observation which I find interesting, is that:
[427](https://docs.rs#427)///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)/// ```rust
[429](https://docs.rs#429)/// # use ::higher_kinded_types::ForLt;
[430](https://docs.rs#430)/// #
[431](https://docs.rs#431)/// type A = ForLt!(<'r> = &'r str);
[432](https://docs.rs#432)/// // vs.
[433](https://docs.rs#433)/// type B        <'r> = &'r str;
[434](https://docs.rs#434)/// ```
[435](https://docs.rs#435)///
[436](https://docs.rs#436)/// is an annoying limitation of Rust, which happens to feature a similar
[437](https://docs.rs#437)/// distinction that certain past languages have had between values, and
[438](https://docs.rs#438)/// functions, wherein they were treated separately (rather than as first-class
[439](https://docs.rs#439)/// citizens, _i.e._, like the other values).
[440](https://docs.rs#440)///
[441](https://docs.rs#441)/// In Rust, `type B<'r> = &'r str;` suffers from this same kind of limitation,
[442](https://docs.rs#442)/// only in the type realm this time: `type B<'r> =` is a special construct,
[443](https://docs.rs#443)/// which yields a _"type" constructor_. That is, it yields some syntax, `B`, to
[444](https://docs.rs#444)/// which we can feed a lifetime `'lt`, by writing `B<'lt>`, so as to end up
[445](https://docs.rs#445)/// with a _type_.
[446](https://docs.rs#446)///
[447](https://docs.rs#447)/// **But `B`, in and of itself, _is not a type_**, even if we often call it a
[448](https://docs.rs#448)/// "generic type" by abuse of terminology.
[449](https://docs.rs#449)///
[450](https://docs.rs#450)/// Which is why it cannot be fed, _alone_, to some type-generic API that would
[451](https://docs.rs#451)/// want to be the one feeding the lifetime parameter: it does not play well
[452](https://docs.rs#452)/// with "generic generics"!
[453](https://docs.rs#453)///
[454](https://docs.rs#454)/// In this example, the only true "generic _type_", that is, the _type_ which
[455](https://docs.rs#455)/// is, itself, lifetime-generic, is `A`.
[456](https://docs.rs#456)///
[457](https://docs.rs#457)/// This is where [`ForLt!`] and HKTs, thus, shine.
[458](https://docs.rs#458)pub

# ForLt in higher_kinded_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/higher-kinded-types/0.2.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/higher_kinded_types/macro.ForLt.html

```
macro_rules! ForLt {
    (< $lt:lifetime > = $T:ty $(,)?) => { ... };
    ($($shorthand_syntax:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

```
type A = ::higher_kinded_types::ForLt![()];
type B = ::higher_kinded_types::prelude::ForLt![()];
```
Produce `impl `[ForLt](https://docs.rs/trait.ForLifetime.html) 1 types

*on demand*.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

- [§](https://docs.rs#full-syntax)Full syntax- `ForLt!(<'r> = some::Arbitrary<'r, Type>)`
- [§](https://docs.rs#shorthand-syntax)Shorthand syntax- You can use the anonymous/elided - `'_`lifetime (or even implicitly elided if behind- `&`) in which case you skip the- `<'lt> =`part, and just write:- `ForLt!(some::Arbitrary<'_, Type>)`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use ::higher_kinded_types::ForLt;
type A = ForLt!(<'r> = &'r str);
// the following two definitions are equivalent to A (syntax sugar).
type B = ForLt!(&'_ str);
type C = ForLt!(&str);
//     Let `'r` be `'static`, this results in:
//                      |
//                      vvvvvvv
let a: <A as ForLt>::Of<'static> = "a";
//     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
//          `&'static str` !
//     vvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvv
let b: <B as ForLt>::Of<'static> = "b";
let c: <C as ForLt>::Of<'static> = "c";
```

# Stream in futures::stream - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3.28/futures/stream/trait.Stream.html

```
pub trait Stream {
    type
```
[Item](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Item);
    // Required method
    fn [poll_next](https://docs.rs#tymethod.poll_next)(
        self: [Pin](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/pin/struct.Pin.html)<&mut Self>,
        cx: &mut [Context](https://docs.rs/task/struct.Context.html)<'_>,
    ) -> [Poll](https://docs.rs/task/enum.Poll.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self::[Item](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Stream.html#associatedtype.Item)>>;
    // Provided method
    fn [size_hint](https://docs.rs#method.size_hint)(&self) -> ([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>) { ... }
}## Expand description

A stream of values produced asynchronously.

If `Future<Output = T>` is an asynchronous version of `T`, then `Stream<Item = T>` is an asynchronous version of `Iterator<Item = T>`. A stream
represents a sequence of value-producing events that occur asynchronously to
the caller.

The trait is modeled after `Future`, but allows `poll_next` to be called
even after a value has been produced, yielding `None` once the stream has
been fully exhausted.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Attempt to pull out the next value of this stream, registering the
current task for wakeup if the value is not yet available, and returning
`None` if the stream is exhausted.

[§](https://docs.rs#return-value)Return value

There are several possible return values, each indicating a distinct stream state:

-
`Poll::Pending`means that this stream’s next value is not ready yet. Implementations will ensure that the current task will be notified when the next value may be ready.
-
`Poll::Ready(Some(val))`means that the stream has successfully produced a value,`val`, and may produce further values on subsequent`poll_next`calls.
-
`Poll::Ready(None)`means that the stream has terminated, and`poll_next`should not be invoked again.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Once a stream has finished (returned `Ready(None)` from `poll_next`), calling its
`poll_next` method again may panic, block forever, or cause other kinds of
problems; the `Stream` trait places no requirements on the effects of
such a call. However, as the `poll_next` method is not marked `unsafe`,
Rust’s usual rules apply: calls must never cause undefined behavior
(memory corruption, incorrect use of `unsafe` functions, or the like),
regardless of the stream’s state.

If this is difficult to guard against then the [ fuse](https://docs.rs/futures/0.3/futures/stream/trait.StreamExt.html#method.fuse) adapter can be used
to ensure that

`poll_next` always returns `Ready(None)` in subsequent
calls.## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Returns the bounds on the remaining length of the stream.

Specifically, `size_hint()` returns a tuple where the first element
is the lower bound, and the second element is the upper bound.

The second half of the tuple that is returned is an `Option``<``usize``>`.
A [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) here means that either there is no known upper bound, or the
upper bound is larger than

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

`usize`[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-notes)Implementation notes

It is not enforced that a stream implementation yields the declared number of elements. A buggy stream may yield less than the lower bound or more than the upper bound of elements.

`size_hint()` is primarily intended to be used for optimizations such as
reserving space for the elements of the stream, but must not be
trusted to e.g., omit bounds checks in unsafe code. An incorrect
implementation of `size_hint()` should not lead to memory safety
violations.

That said, the implementation should provide a correct estimation, because otherwise it would be a violation of the trait’s protocol.

The default implementation returns `(0, ``None``)` which is correct for any
stream.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

`sink`[Source](https://docs.rs/futures-util/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/futures_util/future/poll_immediate.rs.html#72-74)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Stream-for-PollImmediate%3CF%3E)### impl<T, F> [Stream](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Stream.html) for futures::future::[PollImmediate](https://docs.rs/future/struct.PollImmediate.html)<F>

A [Stream](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Stream.html) implementation that can be polled repeatedly until the future is done.
The stream will never return [Poll::Pending](https://docs.rs/task/enum.Poll.html#variant.Pending)
so polling it in a tight loop is worse than using a blocking synchronous function.

[Source](https://docs.rs/futures-util/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/futures_util/future/poll_immediate.rs.html#72-74)

### impl<T, F> [Stream](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Stream.html) for futures::future::[PollImmediate](https://docs.rs/future/struct.PollImmediate.html)<F>

A [Stream](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Stream.html) implementation that can be polled repeatedly until the future is done.
The stream will never return [Poll::Pending](https://docs.rs/task/enum.Poll.html#variant.Pending)
so polling it in a tight loop is worse than using a blocking synchronous function.

```
use core::pin::pin;
use futures::task::Poll;
use futures::{StreamExt, future};
use future::FusedFuture;
let f = async { 1_u32 };
let f = pin!(f);
let mut r = future::poll_immediate(f);
assert_eq!(r.next().await, Some(Poll::Ready(1)));
let f = async {futures::pending!(); 42_u8};
let f = pin!(f);
let mut p = future::poll_immediate(f);
assert_eq!(p.next().await, Some(Poll::Pending));
assert!(!p.is_terminated());
assert_eq!(p.next().await, Some(Poll::Ready(42)));
assert!(p.is_terminated());
assert_eq!(p.next().await, None);
```

# unfold in futures::stream - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3.28/futures/stream/fn.unfold.html

`pub fn unfold<T, F, Fut, Item>(init: T, f: F) -> `[Unfold](https://docs.rs/struct.Unfold.html)<T, F, Fut>## Expand description

Creates a `Stream` from a seed and a closure returning a `Future`.

This function is the dual for the `Stream::fold()` adapter: while
`Stream::fold()` reduces a `Stream` to one single value, `unfold()` creates a
`Stream` from a seed value.

`unfold()` will call the provided closure with the provided seed, then wait
for the returned `Future` to complete with `(a, b)`. It will then yield the
value `a`, and use `b` as the next internal state.

If the closure returns `None` instead of `Some(Future)`, then the `unfold()`
will stop producing items and return `Poll::Ready(None)` in future
calls to `poll()`.

This function can typically be used when wanting to go from the “world of
futures” to the “world of streams”: the provided closure can build a
`Future` using other library functions working on futures, and `unfold()`
will turn it into a `Stream` by repeating the operation.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use futures::stream::{self, StreamExt};
let stream = stream::unfold(0, |state| async move {
    if state <= 2 {
        let next_state = state + 1;
        let yielded = state * 2;
        Some((yielded, next_state))
    } else {
        None
    }
});
let result = stream.collect::<Vec<i32>>().await;
assert_eq!(result, vec![0, 2, 4]);
```

# aegis-id 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/aegis-id/0.1.0

# Aegis ID

Aegis ID is a terminal password-rule puzzle disguised as a very ordinary account enrollment console.

The program asks for a username and password, then quietly adds increasingly restrictive password requirements. Failed attempts only show the requirements that are currently not satisfied. Once every rule is satisfied, the console clears and asks you to rewrite the password exactly.

GraphTrail: a local code-graph sidecar. Library crate exposing the extraction, storage, and query layers so the CLI binary, tests, and (later) the MCP server share one API.

# oxvif - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/oxvif/0.11.0/oxvif/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#oxvif)oxvif

An async Rust client library for the [ONVIF](https://www.onvif.org) IP camera protocol.

ONVIF (Open Network Video Interface Forum) is the industry standard for interoperability between IP-based security cameras. This library provides a complete async client covering device management, media streaming, PTZ control, imaging, on-screen display, events, recording, search, and replay — all over SOAP/HTTP(S) with WS-Security and HTTP Digest authentication.

[§](https://docs.rs#onvif-profile-coverage)ONVIF Profile coverage

| Profile | Description | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Profile S | Video streaming | ~95% | All core operations implemented |
| Profile T | Advanced streaming (H.265, focus, OSD, audio) | ~95% | HTTP Digest Auth, Media2 audio/metadata/analytics config, PTZ compat; Analytics rules and DeviceIO not yet implemented |
| Profile G | Recording & playback | ~85% | Read/search/replay + full recording/job write management; live-source job binding not yet implemented |

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-services)Supported services

- **Device**— capabilities, scopes, device info, hostname, NTP, reboot, user management, network interfaces/protocols/DNS/gateway, relay outputs, storage configurations, system log/URIs, factory default, discovery mode, firmware upgrade / system restore (upload-URI flow), auxiliary commands (wiper/IR lamp)
- **Media1 / Media2**— profiles, RTSP/snapshot URIs, video + audio config, OSD, metadata config, audio decoder/output config, video source modes, unified AddConfiguration/RemoveConfiguration
- **PTZ**— absolute/relative/continuous move, presets, home position, status, configurations, nodes, compatible configurations
- **Imaging**— brightness/contrast/exposure settings, focus move/stop/status
- **Events**— pull-point subscriptions, event polling, renew, unsubscribe, continuous- `event_stream`, synchronization point
- **Recording**— list stored recordings; create/delete recordings, tracks, and recording jobs
- **Search**— find recordings by scope, collect results, end search
- **Replay**— get RTSP playback URI for a stored recording
- **WS-Discovery**— UDP multicast probe to find cameras on the local network

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

- `health`- `health::HealthCheck`, a fast read-only conformance check that returns a- `health::HealthReport`(per-check Pass/Warn/Fail/Skip plus a Profile S/T/G assessment). Pure library code over- `OnvifSession`- `to_json`/- `to_json_pretty`) and a later report can diff against an earlier one via- `HealthReport::diff`- `examples/healthcheck.rs --baseline <file.json>`.
- `mock`- `mock-server`- `mock`module). The- `mock`feature also exposes- `fixtures::CapturingTransport`/- `fixtures::FixtureTransport`for recording real-camera exchanges into- `tests/fixtures/<vendor>-<model>/`and replaying them in tests without the device (see- `examples/record_fixtures.rs`).

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  OnvifSession                        │
│     caches service URLs — delegates every call       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                   OnvifClient                        │
│     stateless — you supply service URLs per call     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    soap::SoapEnvelope  │  soap::WsSecurityToken      │  ← SOAP layer
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                  Transport trait                     │  ← HTTP abstraction
│          (HttpTransport / mock in tests)             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

Two ways to use oxvif — pick whichever suits your workflow.

[§](https://docs.rs#onvifsession--url-caching-handled-for-you)`OnvifSession` — URL caching handled for you

[ OnvifSession](https://docs.rs/session/struct.OnvifSession.html) calls

`GetCapabilities` once at construction and caches all
service URLs. No URL parameters needed for individual methods.```
use oxvif::{OnvifSession, OnvifError};
async fn run() -> Result<(), OnvifError> {
    let session = OnvifSession::builder("http://192.168.1.100/onvif/device_service")
        .with_credentials("admin", "password")
        .with_clock_sync()  // syncs WS-Security timestamp with device clock
        .build()
        .await?;
    let profiles = session.get_profiles().await?;
    let uri = session.get_stream_uri(&profiles[0].token).await?;
    println!("RTSP stream: {}", uri.uri);
    let status = session.ptz_get_status(&profiles[0].token).await?;
    println!("Pan: {:?}  Tilt: {:?}", status.pan, status.tilt);
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#onvifclient--direct-control-you-manage-service-urls)`OnvifClient` — direct control, you manage service URLs

[ OnvifClient](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OnvifClient.html) is stateless and gives direct control over every call.
You fetch and forward service URLs yourself for full routing control.

```
use oxvif::{OnvifClient, OnvifError};
async fn run() -> Result<(), OnvifError> {
    let client = OnvifClient::new("http://192.168.1.100/onvif/device_service")
        .with_credentials("admin", "password");
    let dt = client.get_system_date_and_time().await?;
    let client = client.with_utc_offset(dt.utc_offset_secs());
    let caps = client.get_capabilities().await?;
    let media_url = caps.media.url.as_deref().unwrap();
    let profiles = client.get_profiles(media_url).await?;
    let uri = client.get_stream_uri(media_url, &profiles[0].token).await?;
    println!("RTSP stream: {}", uri.uri);
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing-without-a-real-camera)Testing without a real camera

Enable the ** mock** feature for a built-in, stateful mock ONVIF device and
drive an

[against it — no network, no real camera. The](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OnvifClient.html)

`OnvifClient`**feature additionally provides a bound-port**

`mock-server``mock::MockServer`
for cross-process / non-Rust clients. See the `mock` module for details.[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Cargo.toml:  oxvif = { version = "0.9", features = ["mock"] }
use std::sync::Arc;
use oxvif::{OnvifClient, mock::MockTransport};
let client = OnvifClient::new("http://mock")
    .with_transport(Arc::new(MockTransport::new()));
// exercise client commands — Set persists, Get reflects it.
```
For full control you can instead implement [ transport::Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html) yourself
to inject any fixture:

```
use oxvif::transport::{Transport, TransportError};
use async_trait::async_trait;
use std::sync::Arc;
struct FixtureTransport { xml: String }
#[async_trait]
impl Transport for FixtureTransport {
    async fn soap_post(&self, _url: &str, _action: &str, _body: String)
        -> Result<String, TransportError>
    {
        Ok(self.xml.clone())
    }
}
let client = oxvif::OnvifClient::new("http://ignored")
    .with_transport(Arc::new(FixtureTransport { xml: "<s:Envelope/>".into() }));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#health--conformance-checks)Health & conformance checks

Enable the ** health** feature for

[— a fast, read-only conformance check that reports Pass/Warn/Fail/Skip per ONVIF service plus a Profile S/T/G verdict. It includes a](https://docs.rs/health/struct.HealthCheck.html)

`health::HealthCheck`**parse-coverage**dimension that flags when a parser silently drops list data (a wrong element name returning an empty result with no error). To validate the parsers against real hardware, the

`conformance` example dumps each device’s raw
responses next to the parsed summary so silent-parse gaps stand out.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# rsclaw-migrate 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-migrate/0.1.0

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-migrate/0.1.0/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

OpenClaw data migration module.

Provides three migration modes for transitioning from OpenClaw to rsclaw:

- `Seamless`: coexist with OpenClaw, sharing base directory
- `Import`: copy all OpenClaw data into rsclaw's own stores
- `New`: ignore OpenClaw data entirely, start new

OpenClaw stores data as JSONL files, not SQLite. The directory layout is: ~/.openclaw/ openclaw.json # Main config agents/<agent_id>/sessions/sessions.json # Session index agents/<agent_id>/sessions/.jsonl # Session messages agents/<agent_id>/agent/auth-profiles.json # API keys

# polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/

## Expand description

Utility module for subsystems

Many subsystems have common interests such as canceling a bunch of spawned jobs, or determining what their validator ID is. These common interests are factored into this module.

This crate also reexports Prometheus metric types which are expected to be implemented by subsystems.

# yatrosci_bio_neuro - Rust

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-bio-neuro)SciRS Bio-Neuro

Computational neuroscience: Hodgkin-Huxley conductances, Leaky Integrate-and-Fire dynamics, and the underlying membrane biophysics (Nernst equilibrium, Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz, passive cable constants).

Coverage (canonical formulations):

- Membrane biophysics: Nernst equilibrium potential, thermal voltage, GHK resting potential, passive-cable time and space constants
- Hodgkin-Huxley: voltage-gated Na⁺/K⁺ α/β rates, steady-state gating and time constants
- Leaky Integrate-and-Fire single-compartment dynamics

# agy_bridge - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/agy-bridge/0.5.0/agy_bridge/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#agy-bridge)agy-bridge

Build LLM agents in Rust — with tools, hooks, streaming, and multimodal input.

Rust bridge for the
[Google Antigravity SDK](https://github.com/Google-Antigravity/antigravity-sdk-python)
via [PyO3](https://pyo3.rs).

Rust’s compile-time checks make it a natural fit for vibe coding agents — schema mismatches, missing parameters, and typos in tool definitions (via

[) are caught at build time, not at runtime.](https://docs.rs#custom-tools)`#[llm_tool]`

[§](https://docs.rs#installation)Installation

Add `agy-bridge` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
agy-bridge = "0.5"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
```
Install the Python SDK:

`pip install google-antigravity watchfiles`

`watchfiles`is only needed for file-change triggers; timer triggers work without it.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use agy_bridge::AgyBridge;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), agy_bridge::error::Error> {
    agy_bridge::load_dotenv();
    let bridge = AgyBridge::builder().build()?;
    let agent = bridge.default_agent().await?;
    // Send a message and get the full reply text.
    let text = agent
        .chat("Reply with 'Hello!' and nothing else.")
        .await?
        .text()
        .await?;
    println!("{text}");
    agent.shutdown().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#streaming-responses)Streaming Responses

```
use agy_bridge::{AgyBridge, config::AgentConfig};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), agy_bridge::error::Error> {
    agy_bridge::load_dotenv();
    let bridge = AgyBridge::builder().build()?;
    // bridge.agent() returns an AgentBuilder — chain .tools() / .hooks()
    // before .await, or .await directly for a bare agent.
    let agent = bridge
        .agent(
            AgentConfig::builder()
                .system_instructions("You are a poet.")
                .build(),
        )
        .await?;
    let mut response = agent.chat("Write a short poem about space.").await?;
    if let Some(mut stream) = response.take_text_stream() {
        while let Some(chunk) = stream.recv().await {
            print!("{chunk}");
        }
    }
    println!();
    agent.shutdown().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

[§](https://docs.rs#multimodal-content)Multimodal Content

Pass text, images, audio, video, and documents in a single chat turn:

```
use agy_bridge::{
    AgyBridge,
    content::{Content, ContentPrimitive, Image},
};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), agy_bridge::error::Error> {
    agy_bridge::load_dotenv();
    let bridge = AgyBridge::builder().build()?;
    let agent = bridge.default_agent().await?;
    // Load an image from a file path (auto-detects MIME type):
    let image = Image::from_file("blank.png")?;
    let content = Content::Multi {
        parts: vec![
            ContentPrimitive::Text { text: "Describe this image.".into() },
            ContentPrimitive::Image(image),
        ],
    };
    let text = agent.chat(content).await?.text().await?;
    println!("{text}");
    agent.shutdown().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-tools)Custom Tools

Define tools with the `#[llm_tool]` proc macro — doc comments become descriptions:

```
use agy_bridge::{AgyBridge, config::AgentConfig, prelude::*, tools::ToolRegistry};
/// Gets the current weather for a city.
#[llm_tool]
fn get_weather(
    /// The city to look up.
    city: &str,
) -> Result<String, String> {
    Ok(format!("It's sunny in {city}."))
}
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), agy_bridge::error::Error> {
    agy_bridge::load_dotenv();
    let bridge = AgyBridge::builder().build()?;
    let mut registry = ToolRegistry::new();
    registry.register(GetWeather);
    let agent = bridge
        .agent(AgentConfig::builder().build())
        .tools(registry)
        .await?;
    let text = agent.chat("What's the weather in Tokyo?").await?.text().await?;
    println!("{text}");
    agent.shutdown().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
For full control, implement the `RustTool` trait directly:

```
use agy_bridge::tools::{JsonSchema, RustTool, ToolContext, ToolError, ToolOutput, ToolRegistry};
use serde::Deserialize;
#[derive(Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
struct SearchParams {
    /// The search query string.
    query: String,
}
struct SearchTool;
impl RustTool for SearchTool {
    type Params = SearchParams;
    const NAME: &'static str = "search";
    const DESCRIPTION: &'static str = "Search a knowledge base";
    async fn call(&self, params: Self::Params, _ctx: &ToolContext) -> Result<ToolOutput, ToolError> {
        Ok(format!("Results for: {}", params.query).into())
    }
}
let registry = ToolRegistry::new().with_tool(SearchTool);
assert_eq!(registry.definitions().len(), 1);
```

use agy_bridge::config::{AgentConfig, McpServer};
let server = McpServer::stdio("npx")

        "-y",

[§](https://docs.rs#hooks-and-policies)Hooks and Policies

Control agent behavior with hooks and a declarative policy system:

```
use agy_bridge::{
    AgyBridge,
    config::AgentConfig,
    hooks::{HookResult, Hooks},
};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), agy_bridge::error::Error> {
    agy_bridge::load_dotenv();
    let bridge = AgyBridge::builder().build()?;
    // 1. Register lifecycle hooks
    let mut hooks = Hooks::new();
    hooks.on_pre_turn("turn_logger", |ctx| {
        println!("[turn {}] {}", ctx.turn_number, ctx.prompt);
    });
    hooks.on_pre_tool_call_decide("safety_gate", |ctx| {
        if ctx.tool_name == "dangerous_tool" {
            HookResult::deny("blocked by policy")
        } else {
            HookResult::allow()
        }
    });
    // 2. Create the agent configuration
    let config = AgentConfig::builder().build();
    // 3. Pass hooks to the agent builder
    let agent = bridge
        .agent(config)
        .hooks(hooks)
        .await?;
    let text = agent.chat("What is the capital of Japan?").await?.text().await?;
    println!("{text}");
    agent.shutdown().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
```
use agy_bridge::policies::{PolicyRule, PolicySet};
let mut policies = PolicySet::new();
policies.push(PolicyRule::allow("view_file")).unwrap();
policies.push(PolicyRule::deny("run_command")).unwrap();
policies.push(PolicyRule::DenyAll).unwrap();
assert!(policies.evaluate("view_file").is_allowed());
assert!(policies.evaluate("run_command").is_denied());
assert!(policies.evaluate("unknown_tool").is_denied());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#triggers)Triggers

Run background tasks that react to timers or file changes:

```
use agy_bridge::{
    AgyBridge,
    config::AgentConfig,
    triggers::{TriggerConfig, TriggerEntry},
};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), agy_bridge::error::Error> {
    agy_bridge::load_dotenv();
    let bridge = AgyBridge::builder().build()?;
    let periodic = TriggerEntry::new(
        "poll_status",
        TriggerConfig::every_secs(30),
        "Check deployment status",
    );
    let file_watch = TriggerEntry::new(
        "watch_workspace",
        TriggerConfig::on_file_change(std::env::current_dir()?),
        "Files changed: {changes}",
    );
    let config = AgentConfig::builder()
        .triggers(vec![periodic, file_watch])
        .build();
    let agent = bridge.agent(config).await?;
    // The agent will now automatically run triggers in the background.
    let text = agent.chat("Hello!").await?.text().await?;
    println!("{text}");
    agent.shutdown().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

Note:`on_file_change`triggers require the`watchfiles`Python package (`pip install watchfiles`). Timer triggers (`every`) work without extra dependencies.

[§](https://docs.rs#subagents)Subagents

Spawn child agents that share the parent’s runtime:

```
use agy_bridge::{AgyBridge, config::AgentConfig};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), agy_bridge::error::Error> {
    agy_bridge::load_dotenv();
    let bridge = AgyBridge::builder().build()?;
    let parent = bridge.agent(
        AgentConfig::builder()
            .system_instructions("You are a coordinator.")
            .build(),
    ).await?;
    let child = parent.spawn_subagent(
        AgentConfig::builder()
            .system_instructions("You are a math specialist.")
            .model("gemini-3.5-flash")
            .build(),
        None,
    ).await?;
    let text = child.chat("What is 17 * 23?").await?.text().await?;
    println!("{text}");
    child.shutdown().await?;
    parent.shutdown().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

# sim_lib_surface_card - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-surface-card/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_surface_card/

## Expand description

Shared, plain-data surface-card spine.

This crate holds the codec-neutral pieces of a “surface card”: the
external-name policy used when projecting a kernel [ Symbol](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/id/struct.Symbol.html)
onto a foreign tool surface (MCP, OpenAI, file system, human-facing text) and
a plain-data

[spine that depends only on kernel types.](https://docs.rs/struct.SurfaceDescriptor.html)

`SurfaceDescriptor`Concrete surfaces (for example `sim-lib-skill`’s OpenAI tool descriptor)
derive their external names through [ external_name](https://docs.rs/fn.external_name.html), keeping a single
source of truth for the mangling rules.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use sim_kernel::Symbol;
use sim_lib_surface_card::{ExternalNamePolicy, external_name};
let symbol = Symbol::qualified("skill", "do.thing");
assert_eq!(external_name(&symbol, ExternalNamePolicy::OpenAiTool), "skill_do_thing");
assert_eq!(external_name(&symbol, ExternalNamePolicy::HumanReadable), "skill/do.thing");
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Surface](https://docs.rs/struct.SurfaceDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Plain-data spine describing a surface (a callable projected onto a foreign tool surface). Depends only on kernel types; concrete codecs render it.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [External](https://docs.rs/enum.ExternalNamePolicy.html)- Name - Policy
- Policy selecting how a kernel `Symbol`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [external_](https://docs.rs/fn.external_name.html)- name
- Project `symbol`onto an external name according to`policy`.

# homeboy 0.280.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/homeboy/0.280.9

# Homeboy

Homeboy is a component-aware automation CLI for modern software work: many branches, many worktrees, many agents, and many projects moving at once.

It gives local developers, CI jobs, scheduled automation, and coding agents the same operational surface for checks, reviews, tests, benchmarks, traces, releases, and evidence. Humans get readable terminal output; automation gets stable JSON artifacts.

Homeboy core is intentionally domain-agnostic. The CLI owns orchestration, configuration, structured output, persisted runs, baselines, remote execution, and release/evidence workflows. Domain-specific behavior lives in extensions such as Rust, WordPress, Node.js, GitHub, Homebrew, Swift, and custom team extensions.

## What You Can Do

- Run repeatable quality gates with `homeboy audit`,`homeboy lint`,`homeboy test`,`homeboy build`, and`homeboy review`.
- Produce structured evidence with `--output`so CI jobs and coding agents can inspect results without scraping terminal logs.
- Capture benchmark, fuzz, trace, and review artifacts as persisted runs.
- Coordinate many branches and worktrees with comparable checks, reports, and PR evidence.
- Use runners for hot commands, remote execution, and durable agent workflows.
- Plan releases, versions, changelogs, tags, and deploy steps from component metadata.

## Start Here

New to Homeboy? Start with [docs/start-here.md](https://docs.rs/docs/start-here.md). It walks through the first local review gate, the smallest useful `homeboy.json`, JSON evidence, CI, and where each kind of documentation lives.
